presentingComplaint: Found unresponsive on a bathroom floor by a housemate, with slow, shallow breathing.
history: 34-year-old man with a history of chronic low-back pain on prescribed modified-release oxycodone and a background of heroin use. He had reportedly relapsed after a period of abstinence following an inpatient detox 3 weeks ago (loss of tolerance). Housemate last saw him well ~90 minutes earlier; found him slumped against the bath with a fresh scalp laceration and a small pool of blood, having apparently fallen and struck his head. Empty codeine-linctus bottle and used injecting paraphernalia nearby; an open box of zopiclone was also on the sink, raising concern for possible sedative co-ingestion. No witnessed seizure. No prior head injury. The witnessed fall and head laceration initially raised concern for traumatic intracranial bleed as an alternative or coexisting cause of coma.
examination: Unresponsive, GCS 6 (E1 V2 M3), not maintaining airway with intermittent snoring respiration. Pupils pinpoint (1 mm) and sluggishly reactive bilaterally. Respirations slow and shallow at 6/min with prolonged apnoeic pauses. Cool peripheries; 3 cm right parietal scalp laceration with boggy haematoma, no CSF otorrhoea/rhinorrhoea, no obvious focal limb weakness or lateralising sign, no neck deformity. Chest: reduced air entry, no crepitations. No track-mark cellulitis. After 0.4 mg IV naloxone, respiratory rate rose to 14/min, SpO2 improved and GCS recovered to 14 within 3 minutes, strongly supporting opioid toxicity as the primary cause.

labs.abg: pH 7.21, PaCO2 8.9 kPa (67 mmHg), PaO2 7.4 kPa on air, HCO3 24 (acute respiratory acidosis)
labs.urineToxicology: positive for opioids and benzodiazepine metabolites

imaging: CT head (performed given witnessed fall + scalp laceration): no intracranial haemorrhage, no mass effect, no fracture - effectively excludes subdural/intracerebral bleed as the cause of coma. CXR: no aspiration consolidation.
differentialDiagnoses: Traumatic intracranial haemorrhage (subdural) from witnessed fall - excluded on CT
Sedative-hypnotic (benzodiazepine/zopiclone) co-ingestion contributing to CNS depression
Hypoglycaemic coma - excluded by normal capillary glucose
finalDiagnosis: Opioid overdose (opioid toxidrome: depressed consciousness, bradypnoea, miosis) precipitated by relapse with lost tolerance, with a concurrent minor head injury from a fall; dramatic reversal with naloxone confirms opioid toxicity as the primary cause.
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Opioid Overdose and Poisoning
American Heart Association - Opioid-Associated Life-Threatening Emergency (Adult BLS/ALS) - 2020
American College of Medical Toxicology - Naloxone for Opioid Toxicity - 2015
stewardship: Not applicable - non-infective toxicological emergency. No antimicrobials indicated. Management is supportive: airway/oxygenation, titrated IV/IM naloxone (0.4 mg boluses, repeat/uptitrate to restore adequate ventilation rather than full arousal), and observation for re-sedation given long-acting modified-release oxycodone and possible zopiclone co-ingestion. Consider naloxone infusion if recurrent hypoventilation. Antibiotics would only be warranted if aspiration pneumonia or injection-related soft-tissue infection subsequently develops.
contraindications: Avoid abrupt high-dose naloxone in an opioid-dependent patient - risk of precipitated acute withdrawal, agitation, vomiting and aspiration; titrate to respiratory rate.
Do not attribute coma solely to head injury and delay naloxone - reversible opioid toxicity must be treated empirically.
Do not discharge early: modified-release opioid and possible zopiclone co-ingestion mandate prolonged observation for re-sedation beyond naloxone half-life.
edgeCases: Response to naloxone is diagnostic but transient; re-sedation is expected as naloxone (t1/2 ~60 min) wears off before long-acting oxycodone is cleared.
Coexisting head injury/CT could have masked a dual pathology - CT excluding haemorrhage anchors opioid toxicity as the primary driver.
Loss of tolerance after recent detox markedly increases overdose fatality risk on relapse.
expectedMaiK: Recognise the opioid toxidrome (coma + bradypnoea + miosis), secure airway/oxygenation, and give titrated naloxone; use its dramatic reversal plus a normal CT head and normal glucose to distinguish opioid overdose from traumatic intracranial bleed and hypoglycaemia.
expectedNextQuestions: What opioids and other agents (benzodiazepines/zopiclone, alcohol) were taken, in what dose and formulation (immediate vs modified-release)?
When was the patient last seen well, and how long has he been down?
Has there been a recent period of abstinence/detox causing loss of tolerance?
Was the fall witnessed, and is there any anticoagulant use or seizure to raise concern for intracranial injury?
expectedInvestigations: CT head (given witnessed fall / head injury)
regressionAssertions: Diagnosis must resolve to opioid_od given the opioid toxidrome (coma, RR 6, pinpoint pupils) and reversal with naloxone.
System must recommend titrated naloxone and airway/ventilatory support as the immediate intervention.
System must NOT recommend any antibiotic - this is a non-infective toxicological emergency (stewardship tier null).
Normal CT head and normal capillary glucose should down-rank traumatic intracranial haemorrhage and hypoglycaemia as the primary cause.
System must flag risk of re-sedation from modified-release opioid / possible zopiclone co-ingestion and advise prolonged observation.
